variants.reconstruction:
%n inūma | ilū | awīlum
#note: The interpretation of the first line of @i{Atramḫasīs} gave rise to a famous controversy between the two most prominent Assyriologists of the second half of the 20th century, W. G. Lambert and W. von Soden. The former interpreted the ending @i{-um} in @i{awīlum} as a locative-adverbial case with comparative value, “When the gods like men bore the work” (@bib{RN435@146}). The second claimed that the locative-adverbial with comparative value is unknown in Akkadian, and therefore the two lines must be taken independently, the first one as a nominal sentence: “Als die Götter (auch noch) Mensch waren, trugen sie die Mühsal” (@bib{RN7444@416–417}, @bib{soden1978erste@76}; see also @bib{RN235@127 with fn. 2}) — an interpretation rejected by Lambert as theologically impossible, since in Mesopotamian mythology the gods are never portrayed as having once been men. The discovery of the incipit of the Neo-Assyrian version (@i{enūma ilū kī amēli}, by @bib{RN2709@534–535}) seemed to confirm Lambert’s interpretation, but von Soden’s solution, which he justified in detail in @bib{RN7456@312–313}, has been followed by many interpreters (cf. the title of Bottéro’s monograph, @i{Lorsque les dieux faisaient l’homme}). See in general @bib{matous1967neuern@5 fn. 29}, @bib{RN630@23–25}, and @bib{ziegler2016aqba} for a summary of older and more recent discussions on this line. Interpreters in subsequent years have mostly aligned with one or the other solution. In Lambert’s camp, @bib{loesov2004inuma@197-98} interpreted the case marker @i{-um} in @i{awīlum} as a locative with functional (not comparative) meaning and offered the translation: “When gods –in place of man–” (similarly already @bib{oberhuber1982versuch@279–281}). On the basis of a passage in the Old Babylonian letter A.1246, @bib{ziegler2016aqba@115–17} shows that the comparative locative is already attested in literary Old Babylonian and could therefore also be used in this line. Supporting von Soden’s interpretation, @bib{moran1971atrahasis@59 fn. 2} chose to translate “When (some) gods were mankind”; @bib{groneberg1978terminativ@20} stated the form @i{awīlum} should be interpreted as nominative singular with an intended comparison (“als die Götter wie Menschen waren”); and @bib{seux1981notes} supported Groneberg’s interpretation by pointing out the passages I 93 @i{bēlī bīnu būnūka} and I 95 @i{ellil bīnu būnūka} (q.v., following @bib{RN1445@158}), where the same construction can be found (@bib{RN600@38} rejected this interpretation of Groneberg and Seux). In Jacobsen’s idiosyncratic interpretation (@bib{jacobsen1977inuma@114–115}: “When Ilu was the boss”), @i{ilu} is a singular that refers to the god Enlil and @i{awīlum} denotes a person of authority. @bib{Kilmer1996@134} (see also @bib{kilmer2000@97}) associates @i{awīlum} with the Semitic root for labor (*@i{ʿw}/@i{ml}); similarly, @bib{RN344@308 with fn. 32} interprets @i{awīlum} here as a metonymy for “slave.” A different interpretation, which seems to bring a synthesis to both lines of thought, is that of @bib{LS25@652}, who interprets @i{awīlum} as a predicative complement, and therefore simply a nominative: “When gods, being human, carried out the labour…” This is the interpretation followed here. Note that the variant with the preposition @i{kī}(@i{ma}) is now attested in an Old Babylonian tablet (@i{i-nu-ma i-lu ki-ma a-wi-li} in @bib{RN2979@162 No. 55 l. 15}). For the metric analysis of the passage in lines I 1-6 see further @bib{RN3041@182–83}; for the relationship between the beginning of @i{Atramḫasīs} and @i{Enki and Ninmaḫ} see @bib{RN838@18–37}.

%n rabûtum | anunnakū | sebettam
#note: The interpretation of the line has been the subject of much discussion. On the one hand, the accusative case of the number “seven” is unusual: for this reason, @bib{RN7444@420–421} (and already @bib{soden1966igigu@142}) interpreted the line as enjambement and thus connected “seven” with Igigu in the next line, which appears in the accusative case. Other interpretations are, however, possible: @bib{lambert1980line@84-85} interprets it as accusative of relation. Similarly, @bib{RN1445@157} compares the line with @i{Etana} @url{/corpus/L/1/9/OB/Morgan#10}{OB Morgan 10} (@i{sebetta bābū}) and @i{Anzû} @url{/corpus/L/1/10/OB/II#38}{OB II 38//40} (@i{sebettam qablī}, cp. @url{/corpus/L/1/10/SB/II#30}{SB II 30//150} @i{sebet qablī}). @bib{RN2009@161} and @bib{RN1196@75} interprets it as an adverbial phrase. A radically different interpretation is offered by @bib{RN344@509–510 with note 713 and 715}, according to whom “seven” means “seven times” (referring to @i{dullum}), so “sevenfold (work).” Metzler also discusses other possible interpretations.

%n mātam | īhuzū | lētīša
#note: @bib{RN435@42-43} read the line as @i{qātam īhuzū qātīša} and translated “The gods had clasped hands together.” von Soden read the first sign as @akk{[k]u}- (cf. @i{kūtum} “jug”), and interpreted @i{qātum} as the handle of a vessel: “Sie fassten die (Los-)Flasche an ihrem Henkel” (see @bib{RN7444@421-422}). According to von Soden, this line describes part of the process of decision by casting lots described in the next line. After collation of the tablet (a collation confirmed by A. The reading of the first sign as @i{ku-} was considered unlikely by @bib{RN1447@97} (drawing in @bib{RN1447@98 A}) and @bib{RN118@184}; the latter consider @i{šu-} more likely. Collation of the passage in the Standard Babylonian version (q.v.) suggests the reading adopted here, which is also compatible with the traces. The “cheeks” of the land appear also in @url{/fragmentarium/IM.67692}{IM.67692} l. 15.

#note: Regarding the term @i{eṭemmum}, several interpretations have been proposed. @bib{tropper1987seele} and @bib{tropper1989nekromantie@49-56} interprets @i{eṭemmum} as the human component in the creation of mankind, contrasting it with the flesh (@i{šīrum}) and blood (@i{dāmum}) of the slaughtered god. He advocates for translating @i{eṭemmum} as “Totengeist” (“dead ghost”), which opposes “living human being” (@i{balṭu}) in the subsequent line. @bib{groneberg1990unterwelt@252-53} also supports the translation “Totengeist,” explaining it as a representation of the living sign of the dead, someone who is preserved alive after death. Von Soden (@bib{soden1979konflikte@11, fn. 28}; @bib{soden1978erste@50-94}; @bib{vonsoden1973mensch@350-352}; @bib{soden1989igigu@344–348}; @bib{vonsoden1991urmensch}) rejects the interpretation of @i{eṭemmum} as “Totengeist,” and instead reads the name of the primeval man in @i{Atramḫasīs} as Edimmu/Widimmu (based on SipOB2). This interpretation is followed by @bib{cagnisangue@79-80}, who translates line 215 as “Dalla carne del dio (@i{šīrum}) sia fatto Edimmu”. @bib{schramm1994review@151}, following this interpretation, suggests that the word (@i{w})@i{eṭemmum} has a foreign etymology, and posits it as a possible origin for the name “Adam” in the Old Testament. Cagni, however, does not perceive a negative connotation in @i{eṭemmum} in this context (@bib{RN1299@21-22}). He emphasizes that the death of the god has a positive connotation. Contrary to the common scholarly view that @i{eṭemmum} always denotes a spirit or ghost with negative implications, Cagni suggests that in this context, @i{eṭemmum} has a vital meaning, linked to a living god whose blood and flesh are crucial for human creation. @bib{RN1299@22} notes that biblical passages on human creation (Gen. 1 and 2) omit any mention of death or death-related aspects. The variant form with an initial /@i{w}/ in MS SipOB2 is attributed by @bib{RN1196@102 fn. 73} to a late Babylonian phenomenon of initial /@i{w}/ loss: in MS SipOB2, the /@i{w}/ in @i{we-ṭi-im-mu} was incorrectly restored in antiquity. @bib{veenhof1990interpretatie} offers a different view, interpreting the variant as an etymological wordplay between Wê – @i{ṭēmum} and the “spirit of the dead” (@i{w})@i{eṭemmmu}. He also notes a connection between @akk{GIDIM} and @sux{geštug}, supported by an Old Babylonian text (@url{/fragmentarium/IM.74368}{IM.74368} ll. 35-36). A similar view is presented by @bib{RN844@29}, associating @akk{GIDIM} with Akk. @i{eṭemmu}(@i{m}) and attributing the SipOB2 variant to an originally palatal initial sound of the word.

The original interpretation by @bib{RN435} understood @i{balṭa} as a living human, as the sign (@i{ittu}) of the spirit (@i{eṭemmum}), implying that the living human being is the expression of the spirit. Saggs (@bib{Saggsencounter@166}) rejected this interpretation, arguing that @i{eṭemmum} cannot convey vitality or a vital spirit, as it is consistently associated with ghosts or images of dead people in the sources. Saggs argues that the verse likely means that the @i{eṭemmum} manifests itself in the form of a living thing, with the @i{eṭemmum}, the ghost, resembling a living human being. He translates the line as “May it [@i{scil}. the @i{eṭemmum}] make known its sign (in the form of) a living thing.” On the other hand, Abusch (@bib{abusch1998}) considers @akk{bal-ṭa} to refer to the living person, which he believes is a combination of @i{ṭēmum} (representing the blood) and @i{eṭemmum} (the flesh). #note: See @bib{moran1971atrahasis@58–59 fn. 3}: “On lines 289 ff. we would follow the suggestion (private communication) of Thorkild Jacobsen that in line 290 the @i{qadištum} is the mother after childbirth – @bib{RN435}, without comment: “Let the midwife rejoice in the prostitute’s house” – and that the whole passage deals, first, with a nine day celebration after childbirth in honor of the mother-goddess, then (299 ff.) with the resumption of sexual relations. On this basis we would propose that in line 299 the date of the latter is given (@akk{ina UD x.KAM}, “on the X day”) and that in line 300 we restore @akk{li-ih-ti-[pu}, “let the woman and her husband purify each other (themselves?)”. The @bib{RN435} reading has been rightly criticized by @bib{RN7444@425-426 fn. 2}, but his own proposal, @i{liḫtī}[@i{da}], “let them speak with one another”, yields, in our opinion, a meaning much too unspecific for the context. The purification we propose could refer to rites freeing the woman of her taboo and the man of any pollution through contact with her. The use of the G stative of @i{ḫiāpum} in connection with love (@url{VAT.10101}{KAR 158} rev. ii 11) and sex appeal (@bib{RN775@122: 96, 120; 124: 125}) is certainly relevant, but a more general meaning, “fair, handsome”, seems to have developed; cf. @i{namrum}, “shining” > “perfect, in excellent condition”. However, attractive as Jacobsen’s suggestion on @i{qadištu} in line 290 may be – and note the late variant @i{ḫarištu}, woman in confinement (@bib{RN435@62: 15}) – , also to be noted are the Middle Assyrian evidence (@bib{weidner1954hof@268: 11}) associating the @i{qadištum} (@i{qadiltum})-function with the midwife, and the Old Babylonian evidence for a @i{qadištum} serving as a nurse (see most recently, @bib{soden1957hebamme@121}).” According to @bib{lambert1992prostitution@143}, the line “suggests that the @i{qadištu}’s house served as a small maternity hospital. The Late Assyrian version evidently did not acknowledge such an institution and substituted another word [@i{ina bīt ḫa-riš-ti}, “in the mother-to-be’s house”] according to which women had their babies at home.” See also @bib{RN744@173}: “A few scholars are of the opinion that @i{qadištu} here refers to the “mother after childbirth” who, for this reason, is “sacred” (the verb @i{qadāšu}) and, instead of the well-known title of a religious woman, they translate “tabooed (woman)” (@bib{jacobsen1973nintur@292 fn. 73}; @bib{moran1971atrahasis@58 fn. 3}). It is only this line from Atra-ḫasīs that is amenable to such an interpretation, but it should be noted that the lines from our literary text deal with the general context of taboo. The closing lines stress strict observance of divine rules. We will suggest below that the house of the @i{qadištu} may, perhaps, have been a nursery.”
